title: Density: cork, wood and iron in water, a box of particles (ঘনত্ব)
placement: Book page 131, topic 5.2 (ঘনত্ব): next to the opening paragraph ('ঘনত্ব হচ্ছে একক আয়তনে ভরের পরিমাণ', ρ = m/V), the box with the unit kg/m³ or gm/cc and the dimension, and টেবিল ৫.০১ (বিভিন্ন পদার্থের ঘনত্ব) with the paragraph on temperature.
description: Density (page 131, topic 5.2) on a lab bench with a slate-blue top in front of a warm apricot wall and a teal splash-back. Two ideas, one at a time. First, three balls of the same volume (100 cc) from the book's table 5.01, a golden cork ball, a varnished wooden ball with grain and a polished iron ball, wait on small rings in front of three clear glass tanks of blue water; one tap drops a ball in and it stops where its density says: the cork (25 gm, 0.25 gm/cc) floats high, the wood (45 gm, 0.45 gm/cc) floats about half under, the iron (780 gm, 7.8 gm/cc) sinks to the bottom, and the water rises a little. Water's density from the table, 1.00 gm/cc, decides float or sink. The panel works out the book's ρ = m/V for the chosen ball with mass in maroon and volume in orange, in gm/cc and kg/m³, with Bangla digits. Second, a glass box with orange edges round the same 24 red particles (the same mass, 100 gm): each tap squeezes it to half the volume (400, 200, 100, 50 cc) and the density doubles, with a faint outline of the starting box. The rule grows in the book's words (ঘনত্ব হচ্ছে একক আয়তনে ভরের পরিমাণ; the unit kg/m³ or gm/cc; for the same volume more mass is more density, cork < wood < iron; for the same mass less volume is more density; temperature changes the volume, not the mass). Test tab: 5 questions (ρ = m/V of the box from the labels; which of three same-size balls in water is densest; which of four painted balls sinks, where the heaviest floats; the density after heating doubles the volume; a ball's density in kg/m³), every wrong choice a real mistake with its own note. Phone-first, Bangla and English.
